title: Public Aid and Religious Schools
short: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers chosen by parents; Trinity Lutheran (2017) and Espinoza (2020) held that a state that funds private schools or programs may not exclude religious ones because they are religious.
trouble: Students think the Establishment Clause forbids any public money from reaching religious schools. Aid through parents' independent choices is allowed, and excluding religious schools from a general program can violate Free Exercise.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Can public money reach religious schools? For decades the Lemon test made many forms of aid suspect. The law has shifted in two steps: aid that reaches religious schools through private choice is allowed, and since 2017, excluding religious schools from general programs can violate the Free Exercise Clause. This unit teaches the religion clauses as law: what the clauses say, the tests courts use and the holdings. It takes no position on any faith or on religion itself.

opts.facts: Cleveland's public schools were in deep trouble, and Ohio created a program giving tuition aid to low-income families to use at participating private schools, public schools in nearby districts, or tutoring. Most participating private schools were religious, and most students used the aid there.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist wrote that the program was neutral toward religion and gave aid directly to a broad class of citizens, who then chose where to use it. Any benefit to religious schools came from parents' "true private choice," not the government.
opts.dissent: Four justices dissented (Justices Stevens, Souter and Breyer wrote), arguing that public money was paying for religious instruction and that parents had few real alternatives.

head: Case
Program
Holding
rows: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer (2017)
a Missouri grant program for playground surfaces made of recycled tires excluded a church preschool
denying a public benefit solely because of religious status violates free exercise
a Montana tax-credit scholarship for private schools; the state court cut out religious schools under the state constitution's "no-aid" provision
once a state subsidizes private education, it may not disqualify schools because they are religious

blocks.html: Supporters of these rulings say that treating religious schools worse than other private schools in a general program is discrimination against religion, and that neutrality, not exclusion, is what the Establishment Clause requires. Critics, including the dissents in Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza, say the rulings force taxpayers to fund religious teaching and erode the separation the founders sought. The holdings do not require states to fund private schools at all; they govern programs a state chooses to create. In Locke v. Davey (2004) the Court upheld a state's choice not to fund degrees in devotional theology, a decision later cases have read narrowly.

Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue

blocks.html: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers chosen by parents (true private choice). Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer (2017) and Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020): a state that funds private schools or programs may not exclude religious ones because they are religious.

blocks.title: A grant program
blocks.q: A state gives grants to private nonprofits to install solar panels but excludes churches. Under Trinity Lutheran?
steps: The program is a general public benefit.
Churches are excluded solely because of their religious status.
Trinity Lutheran held such exclusions violate free exercise (strict scrutiny applies, and the state's preference for more separation is not compelling).
blocks.a: The exclusion violates the Free Exercise Clause.

blocks.title: No program at all
blocks.q: A state decides not to fund any private schools. Must it fund religious schools after Espinoza?
steps: Espinoza applies when a state chooses to subsidize private education.
A state may fund only public schools; the Court said so in Espinoza.
blocks.a: No; the cases govern programs a state chooses to create.

blocks.html: Thinking the Establishment Clause forbids any public money from reaching religious schools. Aid through parents' independent choices is allowed (Zelman), and excluding religious schools from a general program can violate Free Exercise (Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza).
